simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #1: Your wallet holds no coins. Coins live on the blockchain; your wallet holds the keys that can move them. Lose the keys, lose access. Leak them, lose the coins. Daily posts on how wallets work and how people get drained. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #1: A wallet is a key manager: it stores private keys (or a seed that derives them) and signs transactions. Balances are on-chain state. Whoever can sign controls the funds, so security = guarding the key and what you sign. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
variant: Crypto #Wallet Security #1: Not your keys, not your coins. But even with your keys, one bad signature can empty a wallet. This series covers what a wallet really does, and every trick used to drain one. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #2: A 12-word recovery phrase is just a big random number written in words. Each word comes from a fixed list of 2048 and stores 11 bits. 12 words = 128 bits of randomness plus a small checksum. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #2: BIP39: entropy (128 to 256 bits) + a checksum of ENT/32 bits from its SHA-256, cut into 11-bit chunks mapped to a 2048-word list. 128 bits gives 12 words (4-bit checksum); 256 bits gives 24 words (8-bit checksum). #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #3: You can't pick 12 random words as a seed: the last word partly works as a checksum, so only about 1 in 16 random 12-word combos is valid. Let a trusted wallet's random generator create it, never your imagination. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #3: In a 12-word BIP39 phrase the last word holds 7 entropy bits + 4 checksum bits, so about 1/16 of random word combos pass. With 24 words the checksum is 8 bits: about 1/256. BIP39 itself notes it misses 1 in 256 errors. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #4: Handy detail for backups: in the English BIP39 list, the first 4 letters of each word are enough to identify it. That makes a handwritten or engraved backup shorter and less error-prone. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #4: BIP39's English wordlist is built so the first four letters unambiguously identify each word, and similar-looking words are avoided. Wallet input screens and compact metal backups can rely on 4-letter prefixes. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #5: Your 12 or 24 words are not your key directly. The wallet runs them through a hash function 2048 times to make a 512-bit seed, and every key and address is derived from that seed. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #5: BIP39 seed = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512(password = mnemonic in NFKD, salt = "mnemonic" + passphrase, 2048 iterations), giving 512 bits. That seed is the input to BIP32 master key generation. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #6: A BIP39 passphrase (the "25th word") creates a completely different wallet. There is no "wrong" passphrase: a typo just opens another valid, empty wallet. Back it up as carefully as the words. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #6: The passphrase is part of the PBKDF2 salt, so every passphrase yields a valid seed. BIP39 calls this plausible deniability: only the right one shows your funds. A typo gives no error, just an empty wallet. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
variant: Crypto #Wallet Security #6: No such thing as a wrong passphrase: type one letter differently and your wallet opens fine, just empty. It's a different wallet. Back up the passphrase too, or the funds are gone. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #7: Same words, other language, different wallet. BIP39 hashes the words themselves, so a phrase "translated" into another wordlist gives a totally different seed. Keep it in the language it was made in. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #7: BIP39 derives the seed from the mnemonic sentence, not the raw entropy. Converting a phrase to another wordlist (e.g. English to Spanish) produces a different seed. BIP39 lists this as a known shortcoming. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #8: One phrase, unlimited addresses. HD wallets grow a whole tree of keys from a single seed, so one backup restores every address you have used or will use. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #8: BIP32: I = HMAC-SHA512(key = "Bitcoin seed", data = seed). Left 256 bits = master private key, right 256 bits = chain code. Child keys are derived by index, giving a tree of keys from one backup. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #9: Your "xpub" (extended public key) can't spend, but it reveals every address in that account and its whole history. Share it only with tools you trust, like your own watch-only app. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #9: An extended public key derives all non-hardened child public keys (BIP32), so it exposes the account's full address set and balance history. Spending needs private keys, but your privacy is gone. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #10: Surprising fact: someone with your xpub plus ONE leaked private key from a normal (non-hardened) child key can compute the parent private key, and from it every key below. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #10: BIP32: a parent xpub + any non-hardened child private key is equivalent to the parent xprv. k_child = k_parent + IL, and IL is computable from the xpub, so subtract. Treat xpubs as sensitive data. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #11: That's why wallets use "hardened" steps (the ' in m/84'/0'/0') at the top of the path: those keys can't be computed from public data, so one leaked key can't climb back up the tree. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #11: Hardened children (index ≥ 2^31, written i' or iH) are derived from the parent private key, not the public key. They can't be derived from an xpub, which blocks the xpub + child key attack at that level. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #12: Wallets agree on where your keys are with a path like m/44'/0'/0'/0/0: purpose, coin, account, receive or change, address number. Same seed + different path = different addresses. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #12: BIP44 path: m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index. coin_type comes from the SLIP-44 registry (Bitcoin 0, Ethereum 60). change is 0 for receiving, 1 for change addresses. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #13: Restored your seed and see a zero balance? Don't panic: the wallet may be scanning another address type. And never type your seed into a website that offers to "recover" it. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #13: Same seed, different purpose level: 44' legacy, 49' nested SegWit, 84' native SegWit (bc1q), 86' Taproot (bc1p). A restore on the wrong path shows 0 BTC. Check the path or use an output descriptor. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #14: Wallets stop looking after 20 unused addresses in a row. If you created lots of addresses without using them, later funds may not appear after a restore until you widen the scan. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #14: BIP44 sets the address gap limit at 20: recovery stops scanning a chain after 20 consecutive unused addresses. Payments past that gap are still yours, but invisible until the wallet scans further. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #15: When you send part of a Bitcoin balance, the rest comes back to you at a new address of yours. That's "change". Your seed covers it too, but a tool that ignores change addresses can miss funds. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #15: Bitcoin spends whole UTXOs; the remainder goes to a change output. BIP44 keeps these on a separate internal chain (change = 1). A tool that scans only the receive chain (0) misses them. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #16: Not every 12-word phrase is BIP39. Electrum uses its own seed format, so an Electrum phrase typed into a BIP39-only wallet gives a different, empty wallet. Write down which app made your seed. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #16: Electrum 2.0+ seeds mark their type with a version prefix in a hash of the phrase, not a BIP39 checksum, and use the PBKDF2 salt "electrum" + passphrase. BIP39-only wallets can't restore them correctly. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #17: One master backup can make many child seeds. BIP85 lets a wallet derive fresh, independent recovery phrases from your main seed (say, for a phone wallet) with no new randomness to back up. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #17: BIP85 derives entropy from a BIP32 keychain at hardened paths under m/83696968' and turns it into a new mnemonic or key. A leaked child can't reveal the parent, but the parent seed recreates every child. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #18: Shamir backup splits a wallet secret into shares, e.g. 5 shares where any 3 restore it. Lose 2, still fine. A thief who finds 2 learns nothing. Keep the shares in different places. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #18: SLIP-39 uses Shamir's secret sharing: a master secret is split into N shares with threshold T (up to 16 per group). Fewer than T shares leak no information about the secret. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #19: Shamir backups can be layered: for example you need 2 of 3 groups, and one group is "any 2 of 3 family members". SLIP-39 allows up to 16 groups. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #19: SLIP-39 has two levels: a group threshold over up to 16 groups, and a member threshold inside each group (up to 16 shares). All shares of one set start with the same words, so sets can't be mixed by mistake. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #20: A Shamir share is not a BIP39 phrase: it uses its own 1024-word list and is 20 or 33 words long. Check that the wallet you'd restore with supports SLIP-39 before relying on it. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #20: SLIP-39 shares encode 10 bits per word from a 1024-word list, end with a 3-word RS1024 checksum, and are 20 words (128-bit secret) or 33 words (256-bit). The spec says it is mostly not compatible with BIP39. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #21: Don't cut your 24 words into 3 piles of 8 yourself. Each pile hands a thief part of the secret, and losing one pile can lock you out. Shamir backups or multisig do this job properly. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #21: Naive splitting leaks entropy: cut 24 words into 3x8 and anyone holding 2 pieces faces at most 88 unknown bits instead of 256, while one lost piece can block recovery. SLIP-39 shares below threshold reveal nothing. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #22: Multisig means several keys must sign, e.g. 2 of 3. One stolen or lost key is not fatal. Keep each key on a different device in a different place, or it's one key with extra steps. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #22: To restore an M-of-N Bitcoin multisig you need M seeds AND the wallet's setup: all N xpubs and the script type, usually as an output descriptor. Back up the descriptor with every key. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #23: With Taproot and MuSig2, a group wallet can look exactly like a one-person wallet on the blockchain. Observers can't tell several people signed. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #23: MuSig2 (BIP327) aggregates n public keys into one Schnorr key. A Taproot output with that key is indistinguishable from a single-signer output. MuSig2 is n-of-n; other thresholds need script paths or other schemes. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #24: Taproot, Bitcoin's November 2021 upgrade, keeps backup spending rules private: when you spend, only the condition you actually used is revealed. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #24: Taproot (BIP341) outputs commit to a key and a hidden script tree. Spending by key reveals no script at all; spending by script reveals only the branch used. Good for recovery and inheritance paths. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #25: A hardware wallet keeps your keys on a small device that never hands them to your computer. The computer prepares the transaction, the device signs it. Malware on the PC can't just copy the key. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #25: Hardware signers keep the private key on the device and only export signatures. The host builds an unsigned transaction (in Bitcoin, a PSBT, BIP174) and the device checks and signs it. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #26: Golden rule: trust the hardware wallet's screen, not your computer's. Check the full address, amount and action on the device itself before you confirm. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #26: If the host is compromised, the device display is the last honest view. NCC Group's Bybit analysis: hardware wallets that clear-sign can expose malicious data even when the laptop is compromised. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #27: Clipper malware watches your clipboard. You copy a crypto address, it pastes the attacker's instead. Always compare the pasted address, ideally on a hardware wallet screen, before sending. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #27: Clippers watch the clipboard for crypto addresses and swap in the attacker's. ESET found one on Google Play in Feb 2019, posing as MetaMask and replacing copied BTC and ETH addresses. Verify on a separate trusted screen. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #28: Air-gapped signing: the device with your key never goes online. Unsigned transactions go in by QR code or memory card, signatures come out the same way. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #28: PSBT (BIP174) packages what an offline signer needs: inputs, UTXO data, derivation paths. The signer can stay fully offline; a watch-only online wallet finalizes and broadcasts the transaction. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #29: Physical access matters. In 2020 researchers showed they could extract the encrypted seed from some hardware wallet models in under 15 minutes with the device in hand. A strong passphrase still protects you. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #29: Jan 2020: Kraken Security Labs extracted encrypted seeds from Trezor One/Model T by voltage glitching, with under 15 min of physical access. The flaw is in hardware, so no software patch. Fix: a BIP39 passphrase. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #30: A passphrase can act as a decoy: keep a small amount in the no-passphrase wallet and the rest behind the passphrase. If someone forces you to open your wallet, there is a plausible one to show. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #30: Every BIP39 passphrase opens a valid wallet, so a decoy (empty passphrase, small balance) and a hidden wallet can share one phrase. BIP39 names this plausible deniability. Defense against physical coercion. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #31: Your shipping address can be a risk. A 2020 leak of a wallet maker's customer data exposed about 272,000 names, postal addresses and phones. Leaked buyer lists feed phishing. Real support never asks for your words. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #31: Ledger's 2020 e-commerce data leak: about 1M email addresses, plus 272,852 records with name, postal address and phone, dumped online in Dec 2020. Wallet security was unaffected, but buyers were exposed to phishing. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
source: https://decrypt.co/53961/bitcoin-wallet-ledger-discovers-full-extent-hack (1M e-mails, wallets non affectés) + https://www.theblock.co/post/88706/a-detailed-look-at-the-ledger-data-leak-and-other-recent-incidents (272,852 fiches, dump du 20/12/2020)

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #32: Connecting your wallet to a site only shares your address. The risk starts with what you sign next. Before every signature, ask: what am I allowing, and to whom? #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #32: Connecting a wallet (eth_requestAccounts) exposes your address only. Assets move through what follows: a transaction, an approval, or a typed-data signature such as a permit. Read the spender and amount every time. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #33: Dec 2023: an attacker phished a former employee's npm account and pushed a malicious version of a wallet-connection library used by many dApps. For about 5 hours, real sites showed drainer prompts. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #33: Ledger Connect Kit 1.1.5 to 1.1.7 (Dec 14, 2023) were malicious, published via a phished ex-employee's NPMJS account. Live about 5 h, drains in under 2 h. Legit dApps served the drainer: always read what you sign. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #34: Dec 2025: a compromised update of a popular browser-extension wallet drained 2,596 wallets for about $7M. A browser extension shares your browser's risks; keep long-term savings elsewhere. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #34: Trust Wallet's Chrome extension v2.68 (Dec 24, 2025) was malicious: about $7M stolen from 2,596 wallets, per the company. Likely cause: a leaked Chrome Web Store API key. Updates are a supply-chain path into hot wallets. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #35: Aug 2022: a Solana mobile wallet was found sending users' recovery phrases in plain text to a logging server. Thousands of wallets were drained. A wallet app is software you trust with everything. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #35: Slope wallet (Aug 2022): researchers found the app sent seed phrases in plain text to a third-party monitoring service (Sentry). It was linked to the drain of thousands of Solana wallets. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #36: Never make a wallet from a phrase you thought up. "Brain wallets" built from memorable sentences get found and emptied by bots. Humans are terrible random number generators. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #36: Brainwallet: private key = SHA-256(passphrase). At DEF CON 23 (2015) Ryan Castellucci showed with his brainflayer tool that attackers test huge lists of phrases at high speed and sweep funded ones. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #37: "Milk Sad" (2023): a wallet command-line tool made seeds from only 32 bits of randomness, about 4.3 billion options. A computer can try them all. Funds were stolen. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #37: Libbitcoin Explorer 3.x "bx seed" used the Mersenne Twister PRNG with a 32-bit seed (CVE-2023-39910). Every possible wallet can be enumerated; thefts started on July 12, 2023. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #38: Vanity addresses (0x0000...) look cool, but keys made by the popular Profanity generator could be brute-forced. In Sept 2022 researchers warned; days later a firm using a vanity address lost about $160M. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #38: Profanity's key generation was flawed: 1inch showed its private keys could be brute-forced. Disclosed Sept 15, 2022; on Sept 20 Wintermute lost about $160M from a 0x0000000 vanity address, likely made with Profanity. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #39: Old web wallet? 2023 research ("Randstorm") found that wallets made with BitcoinJS-based web apps between 2011 and 2015 may have weak randomness. If yours is that old, consider moving to a fresh seed. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #39: Randstorm (Unciphered, Nov 2023): BitcoinJS-era web wallets (2011 to 2015) relied on browser randomness that could be weak, so some keys may be brute-forceable today. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #40: Aug 2013: a flaw in Android's random number generator let attackers steal from Bitcoin wallet apps. Repeated randomness in signatures leaked private keys, and apps had to move users to new keys. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #40: Aug 2013: Android's Java SecureRandom could repeat values, so some Bitcoin apps reused the ECDSA nonce k. Two signatures with the same k reveal the private key. Wallets shipped fixes and rotated keys. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #41: Every ECDSA signature uses a one-time secret number. Reuse it once and anyone can compute the private key. That's how Sony's PS3 signing key was recovered in 2010. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #41: ECDSA: s = k^-1(z + r*d). Two signatures with the same k give k = (z1 - z2)/(s1 - s2), then d. fail0verflow used it on the PS3 in 2010. RFC 6979 avoids it by deriving k from the key and message. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6979 (k déterministe, HMAC_DRBG) + https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_Curve_Digital_Signature_Algorithm (fail0verflow, déc. 2010, k statique chez Sony) + https://www.exophase.com/20540/hackers-describe-ps3-security-as-epic-fail-gain-unrestricted-access/ (27C3, 29/12/2010)

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #42: Guessing someone's key is hopeless: there are about 10^77 possible private keys. Real thefts target people, weak random generators and bad signatures, not the math. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #42: secp256k1 has a group order n of about 1.16 x 10^77, so a random 256-bit key can't be brute-forced. Keys cracked in practice came from weak entropy (brainwallets, Milk Sad, Profanity) or nonce reuse. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #43: Ever noticed Ethereum addresses mix upper and lower case? That's a checksum (EIP-55). Most typos get flagged. But it can't help if you paste a scammer's address that is valid. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #43: EIP-55 (2016) encodes a checksum in letter case using the Keccak-256 hash of the lowercase address: about 15 check bits on average; a random typo passes only about 0.0247% of the time. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #44: Bitcoin bc1 addresses have a strong checksum: any mistake in up to 4 characters is guaranteed to be caught. Typos are handled. Lookalike scam addresses are a different problem. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #44: Bech32 (BIP173) guarantees detection of any error affecting at most 4 characters, with very low odds of missing larger ones. Taproot addresses (bc1p) use the updated Bech32m variant (BIP350). #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #45: Address poisoning: a scammer plants a lookalike transfer in your history, from an address that starts and ends like one you use. Next time you copy from your history, you copy theirs. Check every character. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #45: Poisoners create addresses matching the first and last characters of your usual recipient, then mimic a transfer in your history. In May 2024 one victim lost about $68M this way. Use a saved address book. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #46: May 2024: one person sent about $68M in wrapped bitcoin to a scammer's lookalike address, copied after a poisoning transfer. The funds were returned after negotiation, which almost never happens. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #46: May 2024: 1,155 WBTC (about $68M) went to an address matching the first and last 6 characters of the intended one, after a mimicking transfer. The attacker later returned the funds after negotiations. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #47: When you use a DEX, you "approve" it to spend your tokens. Many apps ask for unlimited approval, and it stays active until you revoke it, even years later. Review and revoke old approvals. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #47: ERC-20 approve(spender, amount) sets an allowance the spender can use via transferFrom at any time. Unlimited (2^256 - 1) allowances never expire. If that contract is malicious or exploited, your balance is exposed. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #48: NFT version: "setApprovalForAll" lets an operator move every NFT you own in that collection, now and later. A fake mint site asking for it is a classic drainer sign. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #48: ERC-721 setApprovalForAll(operator, true) authorizes the operator to transfer all of the owner's tokens in that contract until revoked. One signature, whole collection. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #49: A "permit" is a signature, not a transaction: no gas, nothing on-chain when you sign. But it can let someone spend your tokens. Free to sign does not mean safe to sign. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #49: EIP-2612 permit(owner, spender, value, deadline, v, r, s) sets an allowance from an off-chain EIP-712 signature that anyone can submit. Drainers ask for it, then call permit + transferFrom themselves. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #50: Wallet drainers are phishing kits: a fake site, a fake airdrop, a signature request. ScamSniffer counted about $494M stolen this way in 2024. If a site pushes you to sign fast, close it. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #50: Drainer kits request the highest-value approval or permit they can get once a wallet connects to a phishing site. ScamSniffer's 2024 report: about $494M stolen by wallet drainers that year. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #51: Why can't a "sign this message" request secretly be a transaction? Wallets add a fixed prefix ("Ethereum Signed Message") before signing text, so the signature can't be reused as a transaction. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #51: EIP-191 personal_sign hashes "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" + length + message. RLP transactions never start with 0x19, so the signature can't validate a tx. Raw hash signing has no such guard. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #52: EIP-712 lets wallets show what you sign as readable fields (token, spender, amount, deadline) instead of a random-looking hash. Read them: "spender" is who gets access. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #52: EIP-712 signs "\x19\x01" + domainSeparator + hashStruct(message). The domain (name, version, chainId, verifyingContract) binds the signature to one app and chain, so it can't be replayed elsewhere. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #53: Blind signing: your hardware wallet shows a hash or raw data it can't decode, and you approve anyway. It's like signing a contract in a language you can't read. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #53: When a device can't parse calldata (or nested calls), it only shows a hash or hex: blind signing. NCC Group on Bybit: "blind signing is highly likely to occur". Prefer clear signing; decode calldata independently. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #54: Feb 21, 2025: about $1.5B was stolen from the exchange Bybit's cold wallet. The signers' web interface showed a normal transfer, but they signed something else. The FBI attributed it to North Korea. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #54: Bybit: malicious JS in the Safe{Wallet} web UI swapped the tx for a delegatecall that replaced the multisig's implementation. 401,347 ETH drained. Signers saw the original tx; devices showed raw data. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #55: Oct 2024: Radiant Capital lost about $50M after malware on developers' computers showed normal transactions while their hardware wallets signed malicious ones. 3 signatures were enough. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #55: Radiant (Oct 16, 2024): malware on 3+ devs' machines fed hardware wallets a malicious ownership transfer while the Safe UI and Tenderly showed legit data. A fake error prompted re-signing. Threshold: 3 of 11. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #56: Smart accounts: since 2023 (ERC-4337) an Ethereum wallet can be a smart contract with its own rules: spending limits, several keys, recovery. No change to Ethereum itself was needed. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #56: ERC-4337: users send UserOperations to a separate mempool; bundlers submit them via handleOps to a shared EntryPoint contract, deployed on March 1, 2023. No consensus-layer change required. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #57: Social recovery: with a smart account, trusted guardians (friends, family, your other devices) can together replace a lost signing key. Choose guardians who won't collude: a majority of them could take over. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #57: Social recovery wallets (Vitalik Buterin, Jan 2021): one signing key for daily use plus 3 or more guardians, a majority of whom can change that key. Guardians don't sign payments, but a colluding majority could. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #58: Since the Pectra upgrade (May 7, 2025), a normal Ethereum account can point to smart-contract code and gain smart-wallet features while keeping its address. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #58: EIP-7702 adds tx type 0x04 with an authorization list. Each signed tuple [chain_id, address, nonce] writes a delegation indicator 0xef0100 + address to the account; calls then run that code. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #59: The flip side of EIP-7702: one signed authorization can give an attacker's contract full control of your account. Websites should never ask you to sign one. If one does, refuse. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #59: EIP-7702: delegated code has unrestricted access to the account, and the spec says "there is no safe way to provide this interface" to apps. An authorization with chain_id 0 is valid on every chain. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #60: Delegated your account with EIP-7702 and regret it? You can replace or remove the delegation by signing a new authorization with your key. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #60: EIP-7702: a new authorization overwrites the delegation. Delegating to the zero address clears the account's code, turning it back into a plain account. Delegations are chain-specific unless chain_id is 0. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #61: After Pectra, attackers used EIP-7702 on accounts whose keys had already leaked, installing "sweeper" code that sends their funds straight to the attacker. Wintermute named this contract CrimeEnjoyor. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #61: Soon after Pectra, most EIP-7702 delegations pointed to one copy-pasted sweeper contract that drains accounts with leaked keys. Wintermute's Dune dashboard tracks it as "CrimeEnjoyor". Leaked key = burned address. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
source: https://www.theblock.co/post/356481/wintermute-warns-pectra-upgrade-leaves-ethereum-users-at-risk-of-automated-attacks (1er juin 2025 ; "majority of all EIP-7702 delegations", dashboard Dune wintermute_research/eip7702)

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #62: Not your keys, not your coins: Mt. Gox, once the biggest Bitcoin exchange, collapsed in Feb 2014 saying about 850,000 BTC were missing. About 200,000 were found later. Repayments began only in 2024. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #62: Mt. Gox halted in Feb 2014 reporting about 850,000 BTC missing (customer and company), then found about 200,000 BTC in old wallets. Creditor repayments started in July 2024, a decade later. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #63: Hot wallet = keys on an internet-connected device, handy for daily spending. Cold storage = keys kept offline. Think pocket and safe: small amounts hot, savings cold. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #63: Cold storage: spending without the private keys ever being online (Bitcoin Wiki). Hot wallets (phone apps, browser extensions) keep keys on networked devices, exposed to malware. Keep online only what you need soon. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Cold_storage (définition du cold storage, réserve hors ligne) + https://ethereum.org/en/wallets/ (types : hardware hors ligne, mobile, extension)

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #64: Using a fresh address for each payment isn't paranoia, it's in the Bitcoin whitepaper: a new key pair for each transaction keeps payments from being linked to one owner. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #64: Bitcoin whitepaper, section 10: "a new key pair should be used for each transaction to keep them from being linked to a common owner." HD wallets (BIP32) make this automatic. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #65: Dust attack: someone sends tiny amounts to many addresses, hoping you later spend them together with your other coins and reveal which addresses are yours. Freeze unexpected dust. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #65: Dusting links UTXOs via the common-input-ownership heuristic: spending dust alongside your coins ties those addresses together. Coin control lets you mark unexpected dust as do-not-spend. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #66: Inheritance without handing over your keys: Bitcoin timelocks can add a backup spending path that only opens after a set date, for example for an heir's key. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #66: OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY (BIP65) and OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY (BIP112) let a script add a recovery key usable only after an absolute or relative timelock. With Taproot that path stays hidden unless used. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody

simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #67: Summary: a wallet guards keys, not coins. Back up the seed (and passphrase) offline, verify on a trusted screen, read every signature, revoke old approvals. Follow for more crypto security, one post a day. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #67: Recap: BIP39/32 seeds, hardened paths, Shamir and multisig backups, weak-RNG failures, poisoning, permits, blind signing, 4337 and 7702. Most of these thefts came from what users signed. Follow for more. #CryptoSecurity #SelfCustody
